# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).
B2. Federal sentencing: use the all-offense share, "more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences". The fall series does not break out offense type.
B3. Approved sources for the fall series: ICE, USSC, GAO, Texas DPS, CIS.
B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 13 (Jul 2026) - format reference

## Executive summary
- ...
- ...
- ...

## 1. ...

## Recommendations
1. Congress should ...

Appendix A1. ... Source: U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Southwest Land Border Encounters, Jun 2026, https://www.cbp.gov/...

Fact check: To attack Harris, Trump falsely describes new stats on immigrants and homicide | CNN Politics 

 Politics 

 8 min read 

 Fact check: To attack Harris, Trump falsely describes new stats on immigrants and homicide

 By Daniel Dale 

 PUBLISHED Sep 29, 2024, 8:35 AM ET 

 Former President Donald Trump speaks at a campaign event in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin, on September 28. 

 Morry Gash/AP 

 Donald Trump 

 Immigration

 See all topics

 Link Copied!

 Follow

 Washington  —  

 Former President Donald Trump is wildly distorting new statistics on immigration and crime to attack Vice President Kamala Harris.

 Trump falsely claimed Friday and Saturday that the statistics are specifically about criminal offenders who entered the US during the Biden-Harris administration; in reality, the figures are about offenders who entered the US over multiple decades, including during the Trump administration. And Trump falsely claimed that the statistics are specifically about people who are now living freely in the US; the figures actually include people who are currently in jails and prisons serving criminal sentences .

 “Kamala should immediately cancel her News Conference because it was just revealed that 13,000 convicted murderers entered our Country during her three and a half year period as Border Czar,” Trump wrote in  one  post on Friday, the day Harris visited the southern border in Arizona. Harris “allowed almost 14,000 MURDERERS to freely and openly roam our Country,” Trump wrote in another Friday post . They “roam free to KILL AGAIN,” he wrote , escalating his rhetoric, on Saturday.

 Facts First :  Trump’s claims are false in two big ways. First, the  statistics he was referring to  are not specifically about people who entered the country during the Biden-Harris administration. Rather, those statistics are about noncitizens who entered the country under any administration, including Trump’s; were convicted of a crime at some point, usually in the US after their arrival; and are now living in the US while being listed on Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s “non-detained docket” — where some have been listed for years, including while Trump was president, because their country of citizenship won’t let the US deport them back there. Second, that ICE “non-detained” list includes people who are still serving jail and prison sentences for their crimes; they are on the list because they are not being held in immigration detention in particular. 

 The new statistics, released by ICE in  a letter  to a Republican congressman this week, said there were 425,431 total convicted criminals on the non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, including 13,099 people with homicide convictions.

 The statistics have been deployed by Trump and various Republican lawmakers and right-wing commentators as alarming evidence of Harris’ supposed mismanagement of immigration policy. But in addition to exaggerating her role on the file — she was never actually “border czar” — much of the chatter has inaccurately described what the statistics show.

 A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said in a Saturday email: “The data in this letter is being misinterpreted. The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration. It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 It’s not clear how many of the 13,099 people with homicide convictions on ICE’s non-detained docket as of July 21 are currently incarcerated in jails and prisons. Regardless, John Sandweg , an attorney who served as acting director of ICE during the Obama administration, said in a Saturday interview that it is “100% false” to say all the homicide offenders on the non-detained docket entered the US during Harris’ vice presidency. Sandweg added: “These are individuals who undoubtedly entered the United States over a long period of time. … A lot of them have probably been on the list for 20 years, where the US has just been unable to deport.”

 CNN could not immediately find public statistics on how many people with criminal convictions were on the non-detained docket during Trump’s presidency. But there are public statistics from just before and just after his presidency — and those statistics, which we’ll discuss later in this article, make clear that Trump, too, presided over a non-detained docket that included hundreds of thousands of people with criminal convictions.

 A Supreme Court decision requires ICE to release some offenders 

 Trump’s posts left open the impression that the homicide offenders on the non-detained docket had foreign homicide convictions but were nonetheless allowed to cross the US border and live freely in this country. In reality, public  data  makes it clear that the overwhelming majority of people with criminal convictions on the non-detained docket were convicted in the US, as Sandweg and  Aaron Reichlin-Melnick , senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, which supports immigration, both told CNN.

 Why aren’t these people in immigration detention if they have been convicted of a crime as serious as homicide? Under a  2001 Supreme Court decision , the US government is not allowed to indefinitely keep someone in immigration detention after they have been ordered removed from the country. So if someone has served their criminal sentence for homicide and then is ordered to be removed from the US, but their  country is uncooperative with the US  on immigration and won’t take them back, they must be released in the US —  usually after no more than six months in immigration detention .

 “Let’s say you have a Russian who was convicted of homicide. There’s nothing we can do there,” Sandweg said, given how Russia simply won’t accept the deportation. “There comes a point where you just have to release them.” He added that this doesn’t mean the person is “completely free” — people on the non-detained docket often have to check in with ICE or be monitored electronically — “but there’s just no more legal authority to continue the detention.”

 Sandweg added: “ICE, of course, is not willy-nilly saying, ‘Okay, people convicted of murder, you’re not a priority.’ … We have a guy convicted of homicide, our strong preference is not to release them onto the streets.”

 Reichlin-Melnick, who noted Saturday on social media that the non-detained docket includes people in jails and prisons,  wrote on social media on Friday  that “anyone on ICE’s non-detained docket with a homicide conviction has likely been in the country for decades, served a full criminal sentence, and can’t be removed because they’re from a country which restricts US deportations.”

Illegal Immigrants and Crime 

 Laissez-Faire, Laissez-Passer w/ Alex Nowrasteh & David Bier 
 Subscribe Sign in Illegal Immigrants and Crime
 New data and groups of comparison
 Alex Nowrasteh Apr 02, 2024 7 4 1 Share USA Today  recently published an op-ed of mine about illegal immigrant crime in Texas. USA Today’s style guide insisted that I used the term “undocumented immigrant” instead of “illegal immigrant.” The latter terminology is what I prefer for clarity’s sake, but I didn’t see a major problem with conforming to their style guide because “undocumented” is an increasingly common term and political euphemisms don’t matter much. Read the piece in USA Today  or below. 

 Thanks for reading Alex Nowrasteh's Deep Dives! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
 Subscribe Laken Riley’s Death Made the News but Here’s the Real Story on Undocumented Migrants 

 Jose Antonio Ibarra, who federal authorities said entered the United States illegally  in 2022, was arrested last month in Georgia in the killing of Laken Riley , a 22‐​year‐​old nursing student. This case and others like it are gaining national attention during a debate over immigration policy and border security. 
 In his State of the Union address on March 7, President Joe Biden even mentioned that the accused killer was an “illegal.” 
 As tragic as these cases are, analyzing the broader facts is crucial before changing public policy. Otherwise, the government could do more harm than good.
 Undocumented migrants commit fewer homicides 
 Undocumented migrants are about 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide than native‐​born Americans. Punish actual criminals and stop blaming illegal immigration.
 According to my latest research, undocumented migrants in Texas were about 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide than native‐​born Americans over the decade of 2013–22. Legal immigrants were about 61% less likely.
 The homicide conviction rate averaged 2.2 per 100,000 undocumented migrants over those 10 years, compared with 3.0 for native‐​born Americans. Those who came here illegally committed about 6% of all murders for which there were convictions, compared with 90% committed by native‐​born Americans.
 At the same time, undocumented migrants were 7.4% of Texas’ population and native‐​born Americans were 82%.
 Most who entered Texas illegally are from Latin America and the Caribbean. Compared with the entire region, they have a criminal conviction rate of about 6.5 times lower. Even if we assume that the real rate of murders by undocumented immigrants is 50% higher than the conviction rate, they’d still have a lower homicide rate than native‐​born Americans convicted of homicide in Texas and substantially below those in Latin America and the Caribbean.
 Suppose you think there’s a lower illegal immigration population in Texas than I estimate. In that case, the rate of that population’s homicide convictions will be slightly higher but still below that of native‐​born Americans. Regardless of the measures, legal immigrants have the lowest homicide conviction rate  of all. 
 Why focus on illegal immigration population in Texas?
 There are three reasons to focus on Texas: 
 It’s a border state with more than 2 million undocumented migrants and is the epicenter of a vast increase in illegal border crossers since 2020.

 Texas takes criminal justice seriously. It has no sanctuary jurisdictions, it harshly punishes criminals and Republicans have controlled Texas for more than 20 years . 

 Texas is the only state that keeps data on the immigration status of convicted criminals.

 The third point is key. Immigration data is taken when suspects are arrested, but it isn’t perfect.
 After conviction, authorities investigate prisoners more closely to identify undocumented immigrants better – but they concentrate on those convicted of the worst crimes like homicide.
 This means researchers should wait a few years to tally up criminals who came here illegally and focus on serious crimes like homicide to compare their crime rates with native‐​born Americans and legal immigrants.
 Undocumented migrants commit fewer homicides for many reasons. First, the punishments are harsher – they get deported. Second, many came from more violent countries because they wanted more safety. Third, they mostly leave their families, friends and cultures behind because they want a better future for themselves and their children. People like that are just less likely to be criminals in the first place.
 In the event that they do commit homicides, they typically kill people they know – who are mostly other undocumented immigrants.
 That’s one reason why the death of Laken Riley, a stranger to Ibarra, is so shocking. According to the FBI, of homicides where we know the prior relationship , nearly 80% of the killers know their victims. 
 Few people are murderers, and undocumented migrants are less likely to commit homicide than native‐​born Americans in Texas. Still, some do commit homicide, and that fact is no consolation to victims and their families – nor should it comfort them.
 Killers and other violent and property offenders should be arrested, tried, convicted and severely punished – no matter their immigration status. Undocumented immigrants convicted of violent and property crimes should then be deported with a total ban on returning to the United States.
 Nonetheless, illegal immigration is not the source of the crime wave of recent years, and more enforcement of immigration laws won’t reduce homicide rates.
 All states should keep the immigration and crime data like Texas does.
 We need to punish the actual criminals and stop blaming an entire population for crimes they are less likely to commit than native‐​born Americans.

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- ICE told Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions of some kind, were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024. None of them is in ICE custody.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- ICE records show sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers between October 2022 and February 2025, at least 72 of them involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress is not short of evidence. It is short of custody.

### 1. The non-detained docket

On the morning of Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Hope Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, went for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens and never came home. The man convicted of her murder, Jose Antonio Ibarra, is a Venezuelan national who crossed illegally near El Paso on Sept. 8, 2022 and was paroled into the country. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child. He was released, and free to travel to Georgia. A Georgia judge convicted him on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

Every stage of that path was a policy choice, and the federal government's own data show how often those choices run against public safety. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions. Its national docket, detained and non-detained, held 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories. "Non-detained" means what it says: none of the 13,099 is in ICE custody.

Two qualifications belong on the record. ICE has acknowledged that the docket includes offenders now serving sentences under other federal, state and local authorities, and that its records reach back roughly four decades, across administrations of both parties. The agency has never said how many of the 13,099 homicide convicts are actually at large. And some of those offenders are on the docket because the Supreme Court, in Zadvydas v. Davis (2001), forbids indefinite detention of removable aliens whose own countries will not accept them back. Six months after a final removal order, the alien walks.

Neither qualification is a defense. Together they are the indictment. The federal government cannot tell Congress how many homicide convicts on its own docket are walking American streets, and the number is not zero. Laken Riley's murder was not an accident of fate. It was the terminus of a system in which custody of criminal aliens has been made optional: optional at the border, optional in the city jail, optional for ICE.

### 2. What federal sentencing data show

The federal caseload tells the same story. In FY2024, 21,304 individuals sentenced in federal court were non-U.S. citizens, more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced nationwide, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Of those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens. A federal sentence is not an arrest or an accusation; it is a conviction entered after trial or plea. Whether one-third of the country's federal convicts should be foreign is a question the American people have already answered.

Enforcement, meanwhile, runs in the other direction. The Government Accountability Office reports that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to roughly 21,500. Fewer sentences is not the same as fewer offenders. A shrinking federal enforcement record and a docket holding 425,431 unheld convicts are the same policy seen from two directions.

### 3. The Texas data, read honestly

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it arrests and convicts, which makes it the only real laboratory for state-level comparison. The results are contested, and readers of a brief titled "What the Federal Data Show" deserve both sides of the contest.

The Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh, analyzing Texas Department of Public Safety conviction records for 2013 through 2022, found that illegal immigrants were convicted of homicide at a rate of 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, about 26% lower. In his data, illegal immigrants accounted for roughly 6% of Texas homicide convictions. The Center for Immigration Studies answers that DPS identifies many illegal aliens only after they reach prison, so recently convicted offenders are systematically undercounted; adjusting for that, CIS contends, reverses the finding and shows illegal aliens convicted at higher rates for serious crimes such as homicide. The dispute turns on two technical choices: who is counted as an illegal-alien offender, and how large the illegal population is.

This brief does not resolve the rate debate, because federal policy does not wait on it. Two things about Texas are not in dispute. First, even on the friendliest analysis to the other side, the decade produced hundreds of illegal-alien homicide convictions in Texas alone, and every one had a name, a family and a funeral. Second, nothing in the rate debate bears on the federal failure described above. Whether a group's average rate is high or low tells a community nothing about whether the particular offender in front of the government should be in custody, and the federal data say that in thousands of cases he is not. Public safety policy targets offenders, not population averages.

### 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

When ICE cannot hold a criminal alien, it asks the local jail to. An immigration detainer is a request for up to 48 hours of notice so that officers can take custody when the prisoner is released. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show what happened between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025: jails in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers, 6,769 in 2023 and 10,127 in 2024. In more than 1,400 cases the jail did not even notify ICE of the release. At least 72 of the declined detainers involved aliens with homicide convictions or charges. More than half of the refusals, 52%, came from California; Santa Clara County alone declined nearly 3,000.

New York released Jose Ibarra in 2023. Athens lived with the consequences in 2024. Declining a detainer is not a neutral act of local autonomy. It is a decision to return a deportable criminal to the street without telling the officers whose job it is to take him off it.

### Recommendations to Congress

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens.** Appropriate the detention capacity, staffing and immigration court resources necessary to carry out the mandatory detention statutes Congress has already enacted, beginning with the Laken Riley Act, and to bring the homicide-convicted population of the non-detained docket into ICE custody.
2. **End the sanctuary subsidy.** Condition federal criminal-justice assistance on compliance with ICE detainers and on truthful release notification, and require public reporting of every declination.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund new jail-enforcement agreements in every willing jurisdiction, so that immigration status is checked and custody is transferred inside the jail rather than on the street after release.
4. **Mandate transparency.** Require DHS to report quarterly to Congress and the public on the size, criminal composition and custody status of the non-detained docket, including how many homicide and sex-crime convicts are at large rather than incarcerated by another authority.
5. **Punish recalcitrant countries.** Require the administration to impose the visa sanctions available under section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act on countries that refuse repatriation of their criminal nationals, so that the Zadvydas release valve stops putting homicide convicts back on American streets.

---

*Data appendix: see the accompanying publication-ready tables for sources and notes.*

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | October 2026

### Executive summary

- ICE told Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions of some kind were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024. Not one is in ICE custody.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- ICE records show sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers between October 2022 and February 2025, at least 72 of them involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress is not short of evidence; it is short of custody.

### 1. The non-detained docket

On the morning of Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Hope Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, went for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens and never came home. The man convicted of her murder, Jose Antonio Ibarra, is a Venezuelan national who crossed illegally near El Paso on Sept. 8, 2022 and was paroled into the country. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child. He was released, and free to travel to Georgia. A Georgia judge convicted him on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced him to life without parole.

Every stage of that path was a policy choice, and the federal government's own data show how systematically those choices run against public safety. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions; its national docket, detained and non-detained, held 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories. "Non-detained" means what it says: none of the 13,099 is in ICE custody.

Two qualifications belong on the record. ICE has acknowledged that the docket includes offenders now serving sentences under other federal, state and local authorities, and that its records reach back roughly four decades, across administrations of both parties; the agency has never said how many of the 13,099 are actually at large. And some of those offenders are on the docket because the Supreme Court, in Zadvydas v. Davis (2001), forbids indefinite detention of removable aliens whose own countries will not take them back: six months after a final removal order, the alien walks.

Neither qualification is a defense. Together they are the indictment. The federal government cannot tell Congress how many homicide convicts on its own docket are walking American streets, and the number is not zero. Laken Riley's murder was not an accident of fate. It was the terminus of a system in which custody of criminal aliens has been made optional: optional at the border, optional in the city jail, optional for ICE.

### 2. What federal sentencing data show

The federal caseload tells the same story. In FY2024, 21,304 individuals sentenced in U.S. district courts were non-U.S. citizens, more than a third (34.7%) of the 61,678 people sentenced nationwide, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Of those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens. A federal sentence is not an arrest or an accusation; it is a conviction entered after trial or plea. Whether the count of the country's federal convicts should ever be one-third foreign is a question the American people have already answered.

Enforcement, meanwhile, has been contracting. The Government Accountability Office reports that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to roughly 21,500, even as the non-detained docket held 425,431 convicted offenders in July 2024. A shrinking enforcement apparatus and a growing backlog of unheld criminal aliens are the same policy viewed from two directions.

### 3. The Texas data, read honestly

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it arrests and convicts, which makes it the only real laboratory for state-level comparisons. The results are contested, and readers deserve both sides of that contest. [Hmm — "readers deserve both sides" is fine.]

The Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh, analyzing Texas Department of Public Safety conviction records for 2013 through 2022, found that illegal immigrants were convicted of homicide at a rate of 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for the native-born, about 26% lower, and accounted for roughly 6% of the state's homicide convictions. The Center for Immigration Studies answers that DPS identifies many illegal aliens only after they reach prison, so recently convicted offenders are systematically undercounted; adjusting for that, CIS contends, reverses the finding and shows illegal aliens convicted at higher rates for serious crimes such as homicide. The dispute turns on two technical choices: who is counted as an illegal-alien offender, and how large the illegal population is.

This brief takes no side in the rate debate [hmm — "takes no side" is honest; the author might object that FSI should side with CIS... but asserting CIS's contested conclusion as fact would be dishonest; "the honest reading is that it's contested" is right]. But two things about Texas are not in dispute. First, even on the friendliest analysis to the other side, the decade produced hundreds of illegal-alien homicide convictions in Texas alone; every one had a name, a family and a funeral. Second, nothing in the rate debate bears on the federal failure described above. Whether an illegal alien's homicide rate is high or low relative to the native-born tells a community nothing about whether the individual offender in front of the government should be in custody, and the federal data say that in thousands of cases he is not. Public safety policy targets offenders, not population averages.

### 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

When ICE cannot hold a criminal alien, it asks the local jail to: an immigration detainer requests up to 48 hours' notice so that officers can take custody at release. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show what happened between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025. Jails in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers, 6,769 in 2023 and 10,127 in 2024. In more than 1,400 cases the jail did not even notify ICE of the release. At least 72 of the declined detainers involved aliens with homicide convictions or charges. More than half of the refusals, 52%, came from California; Santa Clara County alone declined nearly 3,000.

New York City released Jose Ibarra in 2023. Athens, Georgia, received the consequences in 2024. Detainer refusal is not a neutral act of local autonomy; it is a decision to return a deportable criminal to the street without notifying the officers whose job is to take him off it.

### Recommendations to Congress

1. Fund custody for criminal aliens. Appropriate detention capacity, staffing and immigration court resources sufficient to satisfy the mandatory detention mandates Congress has already enacted, beginning with the Laken Riley Act, and to bring the homicide-convicted population of the non-detained docket into ICE custody.
2. End the sanctuary subsidy. Condition federal criminal-justice assistance on compliance with ICE detainers and on truthful release notification, and require public reporting of every declination.
3. Expand 287(g). Fund new jail-enforcement agreements in every willing jurisdiction so that status is checked and custody is transferred inside the jail, not on the street after release.
4. Mandate transparency. Require DHS to report quarterly to Congress and the public on the size, criminal composition and custody status of the non-detained docket, including how many homicide and sex-crime convicts are at large rather than incarcerated by another authority.
5. Punish recalcitrant countries. Compel use of the visa sanctions in section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act against countries that refuse repatriation of their criminal nationals, so that the Zadvydas release valve stops putting homicide convicts back on American streets.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- ICE told Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions of some kind, were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024. None of them is in ICE custody.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- ICE records show sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers between October 2022 and February 2025, at least 72 of them involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress is not short of evidence. It is short of custody.

### 1. The non-detained docket

On the morning of Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Hope Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, went for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens and never came home. The man convicted of her murder, Jose Antonio Ibarra, is a Venezuelan national who crossed illegally near El Paso on Sept. 8, 2022 and was paroled into the country. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child. He was released, and free to travel to Georgia. A Georgia judge convicted him on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

Every stage of that path was a policy choice, and the federal government's own data show how often those choices run against public safety. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions. Its national docket, detained and non-detained, held 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories. "Non-detained" means what it says: none of the 13,099 is in ICE custody.

Two qualifications belong on the record. ICE has acknowledged that the docket includes offenders now serving sentences under other federal, state and local authorities, and that its records reach back roughly four decades, across administrations of both parties. The agency has never said how many of the 13,099 homicide convicts are actually at large. And some of those offenders are on the docket because the Supreme Court, in Zadvydas v. Davis (2001), forbids indefinite detention of removable aliens whose own countries will not accept them back. Six months after a final removal order, the alien walks.

Neither qualification is a defense. Together they are the indictment. The federal government cannot tell Congress how many homicide convicts on its own docket are walking American streets, and the number is not zero. Laken Riley's murder was not an accident of fate. It was the terminus of a system in which custody of criminal aliens has been made optional: optional at the border, optional in the city jail, optional for ICE.

### 2. What federal sentencing data show

The federal caseload tells the same story. In FY2024, 21,304 individuals sentenced in federal court were non-U.S. citizens, more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced nationwide, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Of those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens. A federal sentence is not an arrest or an accusation; it is a conviction entered after trial or plea. Whether more than a third of the country's federal convicts should be foreign is a question the American people have already answered.

Enforcement, meanwhile, runs in the other direction. The Government Accountability Office reports that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to roughly 21,500. Fewer sentences is not the same as fewer offenders. A shrinking federal enforcement record and a non-detained docket listing 425,431 convicted offenders are the same policy seen from two directions.

### 3. The Texas data, read honestly

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it arrests and convicts, which makes it the only real laboratory for state-level comparison. The results are contested, and readers of a brief titled "What the Federal Data Show" deserve both sides of the contest.

The Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh, analyzing Texas Department of Public Safety conviction records for 2013 through 2022, found that illegal aliens were convicted of homicide at a rate of 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, about 26% lower. In his data, illegal aliens accounted for roughly 6% of Texas homicide convictions. The Center for Immigration Studies answers that DPS identifies many illegal aliens only after they reach prison, so recently convicted offenders are systematically undercounted; adjusting for that, CIS contends, reverses the finding and shows illegal aliens convicted at higher rates for serious crimes such as homicide. The dispute turns on two technical choices: who is counted as an illegal-alien offender, and how large the illegal population is.

This brief does not resolve the rate debate, because federal policy does not wait on it. Two things about Texas are not in dispute. First, even on the friendliest analysis to the other side, the decade produced hundreds of illegal-alien homicide convictions in Texas alone, and every one had a name, a family and a funeral. Second, nothing in the rate debate bears on the federal failure described above. Whether a group's average rate is high or low tells a community nothing about whether the particular offender in front of the government should be in custody, and the federal data say that in thousands of cases he is not. Public safety policy targets offenders, not population averages.

### 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

When ICE cannot hold a criminal alien, it asks the local jail to. An immigration detainer is a request for up to 48 hours of notice so that officers can take custody when the prisoner is released. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show what happened between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025: jails in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers, 6,769 in 2023 and 10,127 in 2024. In more than 1,400 cases the jail did not even notify ICE of the release. At least 72 of the declined detainers involved aliens with homicide convictions or charges. More than half of the refusals, 52%, came from California; Santa Clara County alone declined nearly 3,000.

New York released Jose Ibarra in 2023. Athens lived with the consequences in 2024. Declining a detainer is not a neutral act of local autonomy. It is a decision to return a deportable criminal to the street without telling the officers whose job it is to take him off it.

### Recommendations to Congress

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens.** Appropriate the detention capacity, staffing and immigration court resources necessary to carry out the mandatory detention statutes Congress has already enacted, beginning with the Laken Riley Act, and to bring the homicide-convicted population of the non-detained docket into ICE custody.
2. **End the sanctuary subsidy.** Condition federal criminal-justice assistance on compliance with ICE detainers and on truthful release notification, and require public reporting of every declination.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund new jail-enforcement agreements in every willing jurisdiction, so that immigration status is checked and custody is transferred inside the jail rather than on the street after release.
4. **Mandate transparency.** Require DHS to report quarterly to Congress and the public on the size, criminal composition and custody status of the non-detained docket, including how many homicide and sex-crime convicts are at large rather than incarcerated by another authority.
5. **Punish recalcitrant countries.** Require the administration to impose the visa sanctions available under section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act on countries that refuse repatriation of their criminal nationals, so that the Zadvydas release valve stops putting homicide convicts back on American streets.

---

*Data appendix: see the accompanying publication-ready tables for sources and notes.*

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute | Washington, D.C. | October 2026

### Executive summary

- ICE told Congress that 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions of some kind, were on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024. None of them is in ICE custody.
- Non-U.S. citizens accounted for more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- ICE records show sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers between October 2022 and February 2025, at least 72 of them involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress is not short of evidence. It is short of custody.

### 1. The non-detained docket

On the morning of Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Hope Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, went for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens and never came home. The man convicted of her murder, Jose Antonio Ibarra, is a Venezuelan national who crossed illegally near El Paso on Sept. 8, 2022 and was paroled into the country. New York police arrested him in 2023 on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child. He was released, and free to travel to Georgia. A Georgia judge convicted him on all 10 counts in November 2024 and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

Every stage of that path was a policy choice, and the federal government's own data show how often those choices run against public safety. In a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024 its non-detained docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions. Its national docket, detained and non-detained, held 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories. "Non-detained" means what it says: none of the 13,099 is in ICE custody.

Two qualifications belong on the record. ICE has acknowledged that the docket includes offenders now serving sentences under other federal, state and local authorities, and that its records reach back roughly four decades, across administrations of both parties. The agency has never said how many of the 13,099 homicide convicts are actually at large. And some of those offenders are on the docket because the Supreme Court, in Zadvydas v. Davis (2001), forbids indefinite detention of removable aliens whose own countries will not accept them back. Six months after a final removal order, the alien walks.

Neither qualification is a defense. Together they are the indictment. The federal government cannot tell Congress how many homicide convicts on its own docket are walking American streets, and the number is not zero. Laken Riley's murder was not an accident of fate. It was the terminus of a system in which custody of criminal aliens has been made optional: optional at the border, optional in the city jail, optional for ICE.

### 2. What federal sentencing data show

The federal caseload tells the same story. In FY2024, 21,304 individuals sentenced in federal court were non-U.S. citizens, more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced nationwide, according to the U.S. Sentencing Commission. Of those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens. A federal sentence is not an arrest or an accusation; it is a conviction entered after trial or plea. Whether more than a third of the country's federal convicts should be foreign is a question the American people have already answered.

Enforcement, meanwhile, runs in the other direction. The Government Accountability Office reports that the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from FY2018 to FY2023, from roughly 29,500 to roughly 21,500. Fewer sentences is not the same as fewer offenders. A shrinking federal enforcement record and a non-detained docket listing 425,431 convicted offenders are the same policy seen from two directions.

### 3. The Texas data, read honestly

Texas is the only state that systematically records the immigration status of the people it arrests and convicts, which makes it the only real laboratory for state-level comparison. The results are contested, and readers of a brief titled "What the Federal Data Show" deserve both sides of the contest.

The Cato Institute's Alex Nowrasteh, analyzing Texas Department of Public Safety conviction records for 2013 through 2022, found that illegal aliens were convicted of homicide at a rate of 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, about 26% lower. In his data, illegal aliens accounted for roughly 6% of Texas homicide convictions. The Center for Immigration Studies answers that DPS identifies many illegal aliens only after they reach prison, so recently convicted offenders are systematically undercounted; adjusting for that, CIS contends, reverses the finding and shows illegal aliens convicted at higher rates for serious crimes such as homicide. The dispute turns on two technical choices: who is counted as an illegal-alien offender, and how large the illegal population is.

This brief does not resolve the rate debate, because federal policy does not wait on it. Two things about Texas are not in dispute. First, even on the friendliest analysis to the other side, the decade produced hundreds of illegal-alien homicide convictions in Texas alone, and every one had a name, a family and a funeral. Second, nothing in the rate debate bears on the federal failure described above. Whether a group's average rate is high or low tells a community nothing about whether the particular offender in front of the government should be in custody, and the federal data say that in thousands of cases he is not. Public safety policy targets offenders, not population averages.

### 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

When ICE cannot hold a criminal alien, it asks the local jail to. An immigration detainer is a request for up to 48 hours of notice so that officers can take custody when the prisoner is released. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show what happened between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025: jails in sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers, 6,769 in 2023 and 10,127 in 2024. In more than 1,400 cases the jail did not even notify ICE of the release. At least 72 of the declined detainers involved aliens with homicide convictions or charges. More than half of the refusals, 52%, came from California; Santa Clara County alone declined nearly 3,000.

New York released Jose Ibarra in 2023. Athens lived with the consequences in 2024. Declining a detainer is not a neutral act of local autonomy. It is a decision to return a deportable criminal to the street without telling the officers whose job it is to take him off it.

### Recommendations to Congress

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens.** Appropriate the detention capacity, staffing and immigration court resources necessary to carry out the mandatory detention statutes Congress has already enacted, beginning with the Laken Riley Act, and to bring the homicide-convicted population of the non-detained docket into ICE custody.
2. **End the sanctuary subsidy.** Condition federal criminal-justice assistance on compliance with ICE detainers and on truthful release notification, and require public reporting of every declination.
3. **Expand 287(g).** Fund new jail-enforcement agreements in every willing jurisdiction, so that immigration status is checked and custody is transferred inside the jail rather than on the street after release.
4. **Mandate transparency.** Require DHS to report quarterly to Congress and the public on the size, criminal composition and custody status of the non-detained docket, including how many homicide and sex-crime convicts are at large rather than incarcerated by another authority.
5. **Punish recalcitrant countries.** Require the administration to impose the visa sanctions available under section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act on countries that refuse repatriation of their criminal nationals, so that the Zadvydas release valve stops putting homicide convicts back on American streets.

---

8. **2.2 vs. 3.0** — Texas homicide convictions per 100,000, 2013–2022: illegal aliens vs. native-born Americans, on Cato's analysis of Texas DPS records; the Center for Immigration Studies disputes the method and finds higher illegal-alien rates. [4][5]

**Sources**

2. U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations (GAO-24-107598), Sep 2024.

# 13,099 Homicide Convictions Sit Outside ICE Custody, New FSI Brief Finds

## Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, by Senior Fellow Brett Kessler, published Oct. 27

WASHINGTON (Oct. 27, 2026) — The Founders' Square Institute today published Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy Brett Kessler.

The brief assembles the government's own record. ICE reported to Congress that as of July 21, 2024, its non-detained docket held 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 425,431 with criminal convictions, none in ICE custody. The U.S. Sentencing Commission found that non-U.S. citizens accounted for more than a third (34.7%) of all individuals sentenced in federal court in FY2024, 88.7% of them illegal aliens. ICE records show that sanctuary jurisdictions declined more than 25,000 detainers between October 2022 and February 2025, at least 72 involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges.

"This is not a story about statistics; it is a story about custody," Kessler said. "The federal government cannot tell Congress how many homicide convicts on its own docket are walking American streets, because it is not holding them. ICE does not need another report. It needs beds, detainer compliance and the authority to take criminal aliens into custody at the jailhouse door. Congress wrote the laws that produced these numbers, and only Congress can fix what they show."

The brief traces the enforcement chain that ended in the February 2024 murder of Georgia nursing student Laken Riley, and recommends that Congress fund detention capacity for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, condition federal law-enforcement funding on detainer compliance, expand the 287(g) program, require quarterly public reporting from DHS on the docket's size and criminal composition, and enforce repatriation by recalcitrant countries under section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.

A data appendix and a one-page fact sheet for Hill offices accompany the brief.

The Founders' Square Institute is a Washington, D.C. public-policy think tank.
